t: Reverse Subarray To Maximize Array Value
o:
We may reverse exactly one contiguous subarray and want to maximize the total absolute difference of adjacent elements. Reversing `nums[i..j]` leaves every internal adjacency inside the block unchanged (the differences are just traversed in reverse order), so **only the two boundary edges change**: the edge `(i-1, i)` becomes `(i-1, j)` and the edge `(j, j+1)` becomes `(i, j+1)`. This means the whole problem reduces to choosing two cut points to maximize a small local delta.

**Example 1:** `[2,3,1,5,4]`, base value = 1+2+4+1 = 8. Reversing indices 1..3 gives `[2,5,1,3,4]`: edges become 3,4,2,1 → value 10, a gain of 2 coming only from the two changed boundary edges.

**Example 2:** `[2,4,9,24,2,1,10]`, base = 2+5+15+22+1+9 = 54. Reversing a suitable subarray adds 14, giving 68.

With n up to 3·10⁴, an O(n³) recompute-everything brute force is too slow, but since the delta of any reversal can be evaluated in O(1), an O(n²) scan works; and with further math the optimum is found in O(n).
k: Reversing nums[i..j] changes only the two boundary adjacencies; everything inside contributes the same sum of absolute differences.
The gain of a reversal is |a[i-1]-a[j]| + |a[i]-a[j+1]| - |a[i-1]-a[i]| - |a[j]-a[j+1]|, computable in O(1).
For interior cuts the maximum gain equals 2 · max over pairs of adjacent blocks of (min(hi₁,hi₂) − max(lo₁,lo₂)), found in one linear pass.
Reversing a prefix or suffix touches only one boundary edge and must be checked separately.

a.n: Approach 1: Evaluate every reversal in O(1) — O(n²)
a.i: Since only the two boundary edges change when reversing nums[i..j], we never rebuild the array. For each pair (i, j) we add the delta of the left boundary (if i > 0) and the right boundary (if j < n−1) to the base value and keep the maximum. This is already fast enough for n ≤ 3·10⁴.
s: For every 0 ≤ i ≤ j < n, compute delta = 0.
Track the maximum of base + delta over all pairs and return it.
a.t: O(n²) — all O(n²) reversal intervals are checked, each in O(1).
a.sp: O(1) extra space — only running sums and the answer.

a.n: Approach 2: Greedy math — single linear pass
a.i: Two special cases first: reversing a prefix nums[0..k] replaces edge (k, k+1) with (0, k+1), and reversing a suffix similarly; both give a one-edge gain checkable in O(n). For an interior reversal spanning two adjacent pairs (x, y) = (a[i-1], a[i]) and (u, v) = (a[j], a[j+1]), the gain is |x−v| + |u−y| − |x−y| − |u−v|. Expanding absolute values into their ± forms shows the best achievable gain is 2 · (min(hi₁, hi₂) − max(lo₁, lo₂)), where lo/hi are the min/max of each adjacent pair. A single pass tracking the running max hi and min lo over previously seen pairs captures the best combination.
s: Compute base = sum of adjacent absolute differences.
Check all prefix reversals: gain |a[0]-a[k]| - |a[k-1]-a[k]| for k ≥ 1.
For interior cuts, sweep adjacent pairs keeping running maxHi and minLo; update best = max(best, min(hi, maxHi) - max(lo, minLo)).
Return base + max(0, boundary gains, 2 * best).
a.t: O(n) — three linear sweeps over the array.
a.sp: O(1) extra space — a handful of scalar variables.

w: In an interview, start from the key observation that a reversal only alters two boundary edges — this turns a seemingly exponential search into picking two cut points. Present the O(n²) delta-evaluation approach first to show correctness, then derive the O(n) greedy: prefix/suffix cases plus the min(hi)−max(lo) pairing argument. Common pitfalls: forgetting the prefix/suffix (single-boundary) reversals, which the interior formula does not cover; forgetting that the best gain may be zero (answer is at least the original value); and integer overflow in C++/Java when accumulating base (use 64-bit intermediates). Edge cases: n = 2 (only prefix/suffix reversals matter), sorted arrays (gain 0), and arrays with duplicates. Likely follow-ups: what if you could perform k reversals, or reverse a subsequence instead of a subarray?
